newsitem.title: JAPAN: Japan unveils details of Japan-U.S. insurance pact.
newsitem.headline: Japan unveils details of Japan-U.S. insurance pact.

text.p: The Finance Ministry on Monday unveiled details of the Japan-U.S. insurance agreement announced on Saturday.
A senior ministry official said Finance Minister Hiroshi Mitsuzuka and acting U.S. Trade Representative Charlene Barshefsky confirmed the details over the phone on Sunday.
-- The current system of setting premiums for the non-life insurance sector, including auto and fire insurance products, will be liberalised by July 1, 1998.

At the moment, an independent body calculates the premiums which all non-life insurers are obliged to adopt, with some flexibility. The rate-setting body will not cease to exist, but insurers will be under no obligation to follow its recommendations.
-- Japan will allow non-life insurers to freely set car insurance premiums on the basis of various risk factors, including age, gender, accident records and region, from September 1, 1997.
-- Japan will give insurers more freedom to set premiums for fire insurance policies.

Currently, the firms can set premiums freely for fire insurance policies that offer over 30 billion yen in coverage. Under the agreement, Japan will lower that to over 20 billion yen on January 1, and to seven billion yen on April 1, 1998.

-- Non-life subsidiaries of Japan's life insurance firms will be allowed to start selling personal accident policies from January 1, while measures will be taken to protect sales routes for foreign insurers. The measures will be lifted by 2001. Foreign insurers have a strong hold in this niche market.

Under the measures, Japanese insurers will not be allowed to sell domestic and overseas travel insurance policies through travel agents, accident policies to students through schools or mail-order accident policies.
-- Life-insurance subsidiaries of Japanese non-life insurance companies will continue to be banned from selling stand-alone medical and cancer insurance policies. The ban will be lifted by 2001.
